title: Sri Rag
hookLine: the first raga (ang 14), serious and grand, often linked with evening

lines: THEN A SHORT SET OF HYMNS.
cards: The Guru Granth Sahib doesn't open with a raga section. It opens with the Japji, which carries no raga in its heading, and then a short set of hymns for evening and night.
Only after those, on ang fourteen, does the first of the long raga sections begin. Its name is short, and it sounds like a title of honor: Sri. The music of the book's main body starts here.

teach.b: What does Sri Rag sound like? In the Indian musical tradition it's heard as weighty and grand, a raga of dignity more than sparkle, and tradition places it in the evening, as the light goes.
Slow phrases, low notes, a melody that won't be hurried: the sound of someone sitting down to say something serious. The Gurus put a great deal of serious speech into it.

teach.h: THE RIVER, THE FISH, THE WATCHES.
teach.b: Earlier on the path you met two of its hymns, the river and the fish, and the four watches of the night. Sri Rag holds the voices of more than one Guru, and of Bhagats after them.
The Granth even comments on this raga by name.

teach.h: THE BEST, IF IT BRINGS LOVE OF THE TRUE ONE.
teach.b: In a salok in Sri Rag's own var, Guru Amar Das says, in paraphrase: among the ragas, Sri Rag is the best, if through it a person holds love for the True One.
Then, he goes on, the True Lord lives in the mind always, and the understanding becomes steady and boundless. Listen to the shape of that. The praise comes with an if.
The raga isn't holy just for standing first in the book; it's worth what it leads to. And what it leads to is steadiness, a mind that doesn't lurch.

A slow, grave, evening raga, and a promise of a steady mind: the sound and the meaning point the same way. So when kirtan is sung in Sri Rag, the music asks the listener to slow down before the words even arrive.
Tomorrow, one of its hymns, sung through a whole night.

how: Ragis trained in gurmat sangeet sing shabads from the Sri Rag section in that raga, and the Sri Rag section is the first stretch of raga hymns a reader meets in a complete reading of the Granth.

o: the first raga section, grave and slow
a festive raga sung at sunrise
a hymn sung only on the Gurus' birthdays

games.q: inside Sri Rag — tap the pairs.

s: the Granth's raga sections begin on its very first page
the Japji and a short set of hymns come first; Sri Rag begins after them, on ang 14.
Guru Amar Das praises Sri Rag with a condition attached
the best among ragas, if through it a person holds love for the True One.
tradition hears Sri Rag as light and quick
it's heard as weighty and grand, slow, and placed in the evening.

games.q: Sri Rag stands first among the raga sections. what does Guru Amar Das say makes it worth singing?
o: its place at the front of the book.
love for the True One, held through it.
games.why: his praise comes with an if: Sri Rag is best when it brings love of the True One, and then the mind becomes steady.

practice: Play a shabad sung in Sri Rag, or the raga on an instrument, and follow the pace before the words, letting your breathing slow to meet it.
If you can't find one, sit facing a window, watch the light wherever it is in its day, and breathe at the speed of a slow song. If you pray, say Waheguru once, as slowly as the raga would.

wordCard.voice: Sri Rag. The first raga section of the Guru Granth Sahib, heard as grave and grand, placed by tradition in the evening, and praised by Guru Amar Das if it brings love of the True One. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, as the heading spells it on ang 14: the first raga section of the Guru Granth Sahib.
